lines.line: Behind me is Oia, a preserved settlement since 1976, with cave houses overlooking the caldera. In the bright afternoon, it felt a world away.
Athens began under a grey sky, the Acropolis still above me. Around me, street art reaches into Plaka and the Historic Centre.
Anafiotika is a small settlement on Plaka’s northeast side, at the foot of the Acropolis rock. In its uneven lanes, I kept looking up.
At Meteora, monks settled among these sandstone peaks from the 11th century; 24 monasteries were built. I watched them rise beneath the heavy clouds.
From this open-top bus, the route passes Athens landmarks and offers multilingual audio commentary. I took in the city from the upper deck.
The Erechtheion was built between 421 and 406 BC. At last, I stood on the Acropolis beside the Caryatids; these are copies.
Santorini’s villages sit around a caldera formed by a major eruption around 1600 BC. Beside the whitewashed building, I felt free to set out.
I drove beside bright blue water, with pale land beyond the shore. The open road made the island feel wide around me.
This lighthouse was built in 1892 by a French company. At Santorini’s southwestern edge, I looked up as the Greek flag moved in the wind.
I leaned toward the old viewing device, curious about the island below me. The caldera is the flooded crater left by Santorini’s volcanic eruption around 1600 BC.
Fira and Imerovigli cling to the crater’s edge. By evening, the caldera islands caught the last golden light.
I settled beside the white rooftops and watched the bay grow quiet. After all that looking up, I could simply stay a while.
